title: How To Use A Vector Database
text:
AI is popular. So popular is Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Machine Learning (ML) functions that drive it, that we have started to look into the core mechanics of AI to know more about how its internal component parts work. With some additional understanding of what makes AI smartness smart, the hope (for many of us) is that we can eradicate AI bias and hallucination, drive AI to do the things we really want it to do… and of course stop the robots taking over the planet (joke).
Central to building the new breed of generative AI functions are Large Language Models (LLMs), complex algorithms that are trained on a huge amount of data of one type or another so that they can recognize the structures, forms and patterns of human language. In terms of where they live, LLMs can theoretically be stored anywhere, but the live best when located in vector databases.
As we have noted before vector databases (VectorDB) are crucial for working with Large Language Models (LLMs) due to their ability to handle the intricate, high-dimensional vector space these models generate. When we say high-dimensional here, we are referring data that goes beyond simple ‘how much’ or ‘what’ value, it can also express size, place in time, its relationship to other values
What is high-dimensional data?
As explained nicely here on GitHub, “High-dimensional data are defined as data in which the number of features (variables observed), p, are close to or larger than the number of observations (or data points), n.”
In other words, high-dimensional data has more features (different ways to denote and define data) than actual data records. As Statology.org reminds us, “A dataset could have 10,000 features, but if it has 100,000 observations then it’s not high dimensional.”
“A vector database organizes and stores vectors - numerical representations of words or phrases generated by LLMs - in a structured way,” explained Mark Nijmeijer, senior director of product, Hycu, Inc - a company known for its multi-cloud and SaaS data protection as-a-service technology.
Just as a librarian can quickly retrieve a book based on its category, a vector database can swiftly fetch the relevant vectors. Nijmeijer says that this is essential for LLMs as they constantly process vast amounts of textual data, converting them into vectors for various tasks like understanding context, generating responses, or finding patterns. Without a vector database, managing and retrieving these vectors would be as cumbersome as finding a specific book in the world’s largest library, drastically slowing down the AI's performance. Common vector databases include DataStax, Pinecone, KX, Chroma, Weaviate, Faiss, Qdrant and others.
Looking at the second player in our list for a moment, vector databases like Pinecone are purpose-built to provide optimized storage and querying capabilities for vector embeddings (i.e. relationships between values). This is designed to provide efficient analysis and retrieval of complex vector data for applications like Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG - the infusion of external ratified data into LLMs to increase AI accuracy), chatbots, AI agents, recommendation systems and also into similarity search for text and images, fraud detection etc.
Now we know why AI needs LLMs and why LLMs need vector databases, how do we choose which vector database we use?
“Before an organization goes on a mission to use a vector database, it must make sure it’s fit for purpose and the use case,” heeded Nijmeijer. “For structured data with straightforward applications, users should stick to traditional relational databases or NoSQL databases. A vector database becomes essential when handling unstructured data requiring complex algorithmic work, such as high-dimensional data, similarity searches, real-time AI applications, or when scaling ML operations.”
Keen to lay down some central parameters governing the use of vector databases today, the Hycu team present the following core selection criteria.
Seven vector selectors
In terms of performance, it is important to assess the database's response times, throughput and scalability, especially if an application involves extensive image recognition or language processing tasks. Looking at data ingestion, IT teams need to ensure compatibility with current data pipelines and formats. For example, integrating a vector database with a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system to analyze customer interactions mandates optimization for efficient data ingestion.
Pinecone says that when evaluating vector databases, companies should consider factors such as scalability for handling large vector datasets, support for real-time updates, metadata storage and filtering, query performance at scale, system observability, ecosystem of integrations and even ‘developer popularity’... which might sound like a flaky metric but is really important.
“When it comes to query capabilities, extensive query functions (such as nearest neighbour search, range queries and similarity assessments) are crucial. A content recommendation system, for example, relies heavily on complex similarity searches for personalized user experiences,” noted Hycu’s Nijmeijer. “Then we come to indexing, organizations must choose a database that offers efficient storage and quick retrieval of vector data, especially for uses such as image recognition applications where quick indexing and retrieval of images based on visual similarity are vital.”
The buck obviously often stops with cost, so there is a need to consider the vector database’s licensing costs and the total cost of ownership. Smaller organizations are often advised to focus on cost optimization when developing internal chatbots that make use of vector technologies that run in line with LLMs in the realm of AI.
Data protection & security
An analysis of vector database options would be incomplete without a mention of data protection i.e. a business needs to plan for contingencies such as deletions, misconfigurations or cyber-attacks by selecting a vendor with robust recovery capabilities or support from third-party protection and recovery solutions. This is especially critical for retail or e-commerce, where downtime is not an option.
“Finally (although we could make this list longer quite easily if needed) we come to security,” said Nijmeijer. “For organizations with stringent security and compliance requirements, choosing a vector database that satisfies data sovereignty needs is imperative. Identify and align with your organization's data residency, access and retention policies. Healthcare-related applications, for example, must place security at the forefront of their vector database selection criteria.”
While we have covered the fundamentals here, it’s worth remembering that the vector marketplace is moving as fast as the LLM and AI space in general. As an additional caveat, we might suggest that organizations should opt for vector technology choices that not only fit their technical requirements but also aligns with your organizational needs and constraints.
Is vector-washing a thing?
It’s also worth considering the fact that every company that is a database company may now be quite happy to style itself as a vector database company, so look at where vendors have come from and at what point they have evolved. Vector-washing (like greenwashing, open source washing or other) is not a thing yet, but it could be, so stay alert and consider every vector of choice (the deliberate use of cheesy callback term apologized for) in this equation.
“When traditional database companies see the explosive growth and demand for vector databases as part of AI workloads, it's hard to fault them for trying to get in on the action,” said Greg Kogan, VP of marketing & growth at Pinecone. “But history has shown time and again that the best applications are built on databases purpose-built for the data types and query patterns those applications rely on. With AI applications the dominant data types are vectors and the query patterns are vector search. The difference may be hard to spot with very small use cases, but the difference in performance, cost efficiency and reliability is very clear when working with anything past a sample application."
Kogan reminds us that software developers are racing to build differentiated and commercially viable AI applications; this means they need more than just access to LLMs and vector search to achieve that. The key (as the team at Pinecone says it has found), is to give AI applications on-demand access to the company's data i.e. the more data it can search through semantically to find the right context, the better the application performs in terms of answer quality.
The takeaways here appear to centralize on the need to use the right tool for the job, a maxim which in this scenario translates to ‘use a database that designed from the ground up to be fit for AI-centric purpose’ and to put provisioning for scale (AI is big and getting bigger, just in case you hadn’t noticed) even a business is still in experimentation mode with AI.

title: South Korea's Yoon, Meta's Zuckerberg discuss AI, digital ecosystems - ET Telecom

South Korea's Yoon, Meta's Zuckerberg discuss AI, digital ecosystems
The president also promised support for business tie ups and expressed hope for greater collaboration in areas like the metaverse and extended reality (XR) headsets, it said.
By Hyonhee Shin and Joyce Lee
SEOUL: South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol met Meta's CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Thursday for talks to explore ways to increase cooperation with the U.S. company in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital ecosystems, Yoon's office said.
Yoon said South Korea's portfolio of smart home appliances, wearable devices and smart cars offered a good platform for Meta's AI technology.
The president also promised support for business tie ups and expressed hope for greater collaboration in areas like the metaverse and extended reality (XR) headsets, it said.
"The two discussed the vision for creating open AI and digital ecosystems and how to strengthen cooperation between Meta and our companies," Yoon's policy chief, Sung Tae-yoon, told a briefing.
"The president said that the Korean industry is ready to actively support what Meta has imagined and designed."
Yoon also asked Meta to play an active role monitoring and countering fake news and other malpractices on its platforms as many countries gear up for elections this year, Sung said.
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On Wednesday, Zuckerberg met Samsung Electronics Chairman Jay Y. Lee and LG Electronics CEO William Cho to discuss potential cooperation in AI and XR technology.
Meta launched its latest mixed-reality headset, Quest 3, in June before rival Apple ramped up competition this month with its Vision Pro device.
AI chip supply and expanding ecosystems for generative AI are key priorities for Meta this year, as the company seeks to get generative AI technology into its social media products and hardware devices.

South Korea will host a global AI Safety Summit in May.

title: Council Post: Mastering Risk: Unleashing The Power Of Data And AI In Strategic Risk Management
text:
Sal Rehmetullah is the founder of Stax Payments, a Unicorn in the Fintech space, and serial entrepreneur.
In the intricate realm of contemporary business, the mastery of risk management hinges on the strategic utilization of data and artificial intelligence. I wanted to dive into this transformative landscape and focus on four pivotal insights that illuminate how harnessing data and AI can fortify risk management strategies.
In the last few years, the emergence of AI has continued to find its way into organizations. As an executive leading multiple revenue streams, divisions and global offices, having the right data is important, but being able to analyze it in real time to drive strategic decision-making can be difficult. As organizations grow, risk management becomes just as important for growth.
1. Data-Driven Cartography: Navigating Risks With Precision
To chart the nuanced landscape of risk, businesses are increasingly turning to advanced risk assessment tools infused with AI capabilities. These tools, such as IBM's Watson Analytics and SAS Enterprise Miner, harness the power of machine learning algorithms to analyze vast datasets, identifying patterns and correlations that might elude traditional methods.
This data-driven cartography provides a comprehensive understanding of financial intricacies, operational nuances and external market dynamics, paving the way for proactive risk identification. This strategy can be applied to all business types. With the complexities continuing to grow inside businesses, it's important to not only leverage the power of data but also find a way to get value out of it.
2. AI As The Strategic Vanguard: Anticipating Challenges In Real Time
Predictive analytics platforms, like Salesforce Einstein Analytics and Google Cloud AI, exemplify the transformative impact of AI in anticipating challenges. By analyzing historical data and recognizing patterns, these platforms enable organizations to predict potential risks and market trends.
For instance, a retail company leveraging AI might anticipate shifts in consumer behavior during economic downturns, allowing it to adjust inventory levels proactively. This type of proactive behavior is where the future is heading. It's no longer about risk management up front but instead about how you can better predict the good, the bad and/or the ugly to help grow your business.
3. Collaborative Intelligence: Fostering A Unified Front In Risk Management
Internal reporting systems enhanced by AI not only streamline communication but also elevate collective intelligence. Tools like Microsoft Power BI and Tableau leverage AI to turn raw data into interactive visualizations. This fosters a culture of collective responsibility, allowing stakeholders to interpret and share insights across departments seamlessly.
Imagine a scenario where a manufacturing firm utilizes AI-driven reporting tools to identify supply chain vulnerabilities, enabling a swift, collaborative response to potential disruptions. This also enables and empowers each of the organizational members to do more with their time and focus on key priorities.
4. Technological Allies: Data And AI As Strategic Assets
In the arsenal of risk management, cutting-edge tools like risk analytics platforms and machine learning solutions serve as technological allies. Consider Palantir's Foundry or AWS SageMaker; these platforms empower organizations to turn data into actionable insights.
An insurance company, for example, could utilize AI-driven risk analytics to assess policyholder behavior and market trends, optimizing underwriting processes and enhancing overall risk management efficacy.
Ensure you set up the right data management strategy and how to use it at your organization. Start with building a KPI sheet to model out risk elements and key predicting indicators to not only drive your business forward, but also to protect it.
As your organization embraces these examples and tools, the symbiotic relationship between data and AI becomes the bedrock of strategic risk management. The narrative of modern risk management is not only about navigating uncertainties but leveraging these technological advancements to transform challenges into opportunities for growth and resilience in an ever-evolving business landscape.

title: Council Post: No, AI Won’t Kill PR: How To Be An Expert In The AI Age
text:
Lydia is a key contributor to brands’ ongoing success as Senior VP of Elevate at ChicExecs.
The release of ChatGPT in November of 2022 created hysteria over artificial intelligence (AI). Over a year later, it’s clear that the robot overlords aren’t gunning for our jobs. If anything, AI takes less-than-fun tasks off our plates so we can focus on more value-added tasks.
AI might continue to make headlines, but the proliferation of generic AI content has left a massive void in the market. There’s an emerging need for human experts to provide context, share their informed opinions and guide discourse. In an era when anyone can ask ChatGPT to spit out (potentially incorrect) information, it’s never been more critical for human experts to position themselves as forerunners and thought leaders.
Posting on social media and writing blogs will get you far, but when you want to make a memorable impression in the AI age, get a public relations (PR) team in your corner. In this article, I’ll explain why expertise is so valuable today and how you can leverage it with custom-tailored PR strategies.
The Indispensable Role Of Expertise In 2024 And Beyond
AI can process information at the speed of light, but it can’t make moral judgments or offer nuanced perspectives like an expert can. Whether you’re a doctor, business owner, inventor or hairstylist, you have years of expertise that even the most well-trained chatbot can’t replace. For every AI breakthrough, there’s context, backstory and implications that need deciphering—and that’s where you come in.
Experts provide clarity in the noise that is the internet. Your deep understanding of the field makes complex topics more accessible to the public, which has real value. If you play your cards right, you can create an AI-proof marketing strategy that positions you as an industry authority.
How To Leverage PR To Amplify Your Expertise
You know you want to be an authority, but how do you get others to recognize you as an expert? Having expertise is only part of the equation. Broadcasting that expertise to the right audience, in the right place, at the right time is just as important.
This is where PR comes into play. Agencies craft personalized marketing and PR campaigns to get the word out, share your expertise and promote your brand. It won’t happen overnight, but these strategies help to amplify your expertise—even in the age of AI.
Identify your core message and create content around it.
What’s your area of expertise? What do you stand for? You might have expert skincare knowledge, for example, but you’ll get more traction by specializing in a specific niche, like wrinkle prevention and treatment. As long as the audience is large enough, becoming an expert in a specific niche is a great way to build a reputation in your industry quickly.
Once you decide on your core message, make a plan to share that information in multiple formats, including:
• Blogs.
• White papers.
• Webinars.
• Podcasts.
A solid PR agency will work with you to create consistent messaging and generate more content for your brand. This includes sending out press releases, securing press mentions and even scheduling media interviews.
Invest in media training.
You’re an expert, but you still need to “seem” like an expert to your audience. The classic combination of logos (logic), pathos (emotion) and ethos (authority) is a must-have for positioning yourself as a trustworthy expert.
A good PR team will coach you on how to speak, dress and interact with the press. It might seem like a minor consideration right now, but media training will help you look more polished and trustworthy, which is a must for bolstering trust.
Submit for awards.
ChatGPT can do a lot, but we’re willing to bet it doesn’t have industry accolades. Awards are a type of recognition from industry bodies that elevate your standing. Work with your PR team to identify award submissions. They’ll create a strategy not only for applying for awards but also to help you complete projects that you can use for award submissions down the line.
Give in-person talks.
You’re competing with AI content online. But AI still can’t replicate in-person talks, so it’s critical for you to speak at conferences, panels and seminars. The more specialized, the better. Your PR team will work with you to identify events and speaking opportunities that give you the best chance to share your domain expertise.
Harnessing Human Ingenuity In An AI-Driven World
As a living, breathing expert, you have something that’s truly AI-proof. You have the expertise; all you need is a team with the skills, tools and relationships to convert that expertise into value.

title: Council Post: The Role Of AI In Managing Vehicle Data And Simplifying Analytics
text:
Mayank Sikaria is President & cofounder of Sibros, a connected vehicle data management & OTA software update company.
When we think of artificial intelligence (AI) in automotive, we often jump straight to self-driving cars, a personalized in-vehicle experience and enhanced safety. However, before we can arrive at an automobile that adapts to our immediate needs or handles our daily commute, we need to look at the fuel that feeds the algorithms—vehicle data.
Understanding Vehicle Data Complexity
Over the last decade, data generation in the automotive industry has gone through the roof. In 2014, McKinsey estimated that some connected cars were generating around 25 gigabytes of data per hour, a number that at the time was considered massive. However, research from Lucid Motors (via Visual Capitalist) suggests that modern software-defined vehicles (SDVs) produce anywhere between 1.4 terabytes and 19 terabytes of data an hour. That's an increase of over 5,000% in just 10 years.
Factors behind this escalation include an increase in sensors (including cameras, lidar and radar), high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and advanced vehicle architectures—all of which have been integrated to accommodate more advanced vehicle capabilities and consumer needs.
The trouble, however, is not the amount of data these systems produce but, rather, how to access and sort the relevant data from the superfluous—a task that can be both challenging and expensive. By leveraging innovative data logging approaches, automakers can eliminate some of the irrelevant data before relaying it to the cloud. However, the true power behind data management and analytics is AI. While the potential use cases for AI-driven data management and analytics are extensive, we will focus on three in particular.
Case Studies For AI-Driven Data Analytics
Fault Analysis
Vehicle faults occur for any number of reasons: manufacturing defects, incorrect software versions, unexpected system glitches, improper maintenance, and normal wear and tear. Naturally, the cause of a fault is not always clear, nor is the solution.
Depending on the fault's severity, it might be necessary to issue a recall notice—which can cost the automaker hundreds to thousands of dollars per vehicle. Unfortunately, recall scopes are based on a "best guess" in which all vehicles that may be impacted are recalled. This approach is both expensive and time-consuming.
An alternative is to use AI to isolate patterns among vehicles exhibiting faults and drill down their occurrences to determine if they are occurring:
• On a particular software version.
• In a particular geographical region.
• On a specific make or model.
• On vehicles that share a specific attribute.
This not only narrows the scope but expedites fault identification and analysis, saving the automaker both time and money. A 2022 SAE International article discussed this type of use case, in which a method that leveraged AI and machine learning was used to predict a vehicle fault before it happened.
Driver Training
Today, fleet managers and insurance companies base driver scores on how good or bad driving behavior is. However, these scores are often based on a limited number of data points and include no insights for improvement.
AI-driven data analytics can assess driving behaviors based on a wider range of data points and offer vehicle-level personalized recommendations for improvement. Researchers in Beijing experimented with using AI in driver training systems in 2019.
Fostering better driving via real-world insights can not only increase road safety, but it can also lead to optimized vehicle utilization and prolonged operation. In other words, using AI for vehicle data analytics can reduce the total cost of ownership for the fleet manager and insurance premiums for the independent driver. When looking at electric vehicles (EVs) specifically, better driving can also result in a lower battery degradation rate, which in turn increases the vehicle's ability to maintain its range over time.
Reductive Design
An issue that plagues many EV original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) is battery size. Similar to recalls, EV battery size has traditionally been based on estimations. Automakers make assumptions about the needs of the user and select the battery capacity accordingly. However, by leveraging AI to analyze real-world data such as driving and charging patterns, OEMs can determine whether the battery is oversized, undersized or just right for their target market.
They can also determine how certain owner behaviors impact the life of the battery, such as the distance a vehicle covers between charging cycles, the charge frequency and regularity, and the extent of discharge before charging. OEMs can use this information to make product adjustments and provide guidance to users to help increase battery and vehicle longevity.
Outside of battery sizing, automakers can leverage data to remove underused features. Ford announced in February 2024 that it was removing its driver-assist parallel parking feature based on a data analysis revealing that most customers weren't using it. By adjusting design based on actual usage information, OEMs can reduce production and vehicle costs, ultimately leading to higher sales.
Potential Challenges
While there is huge potential for AI-driven analytics and vehicle data management, there are still several challenges and limitations that must be addressed.
AI requires massive computational resources to function, including storage, memory and power. It is also susceptible to data privacy concerns such as how user data is protected or how systems are secured against biased algorithms and data. As AI in automotive continues to evolve, we will likely see increased legislation that helps address these issues and ensures protection for drivers and their data.
AI And The Automotive Future
There's no telling how much data SDVs will be producing 10 years from now, but one thing we do know is that AI will prove instrumental in simplifying vehicle data management and analytics. It has the potential to cut through irrelevant data and provide insightful and actionable insights to improve vehicle safety, efficiency and functionality. One day, we will likely see generative AI creating a more holistic and intuitive driving experience where both driver and vehicle can learn from each other.

title: AI Hallucinations Said To Be Proven As Unavoidably Inevitable But Don’t Unduly Despair Since They Are Hopefully Detectable And Likely Correctable
text:
In today’s column, I am focusing on the topic of so-called AI hallucinations, which is a widely adopted phrase referring to circumstances whereby generative AI seemingly at times makes up fictitious indications in response to user prompts. A new research study has dropped what some might consider a bombshell about AI hallucinations. Hang in there as I unveil the latest said-to-be shocking news.
I’ll cover the essence of the study and provide you with insightful commentary about what the results portend and what your best takeaways ought to be. For my prior coverage on the vaunted topic of AI hallucinations, take a look at the link here, the link here, and the link here, just to name a few.
I will start with a heads-up overview and then walk you through the receipts that provide support to my remarks.
Buckle up for a wild ride.
Run Amok Or Use Our Brains To Suitably React
The recent study that I’ll in a moment be quoting from has asserted that AI hallucinations are unavoidably inevitable.
Yikes, the kneejerk reaction appears to be, watch out since we are doomed to a lifetime of enduring AI hallucinations in generative AI. You apparently would be wise to shut your curtains and close your doors. The boogeyman of AI hallucinations is here to stay. Woe is us. Woe is humankind.
Please prepare yourself for something that might seem triggering.
I consider the study to be a semblance of good news.
Say what?
Yes, I am excited that a rigorous study has landed on a result that I and others have been proffering as an educated guess for quite a while now. Those outsized aims of driving AI hallucinations to zero is not a realistic goal. Fess up and open your eyes. Zero is just not a sensibility worthy of ongoing angst and edge-of-your-seat hopes.
Do not misunderstand that contention. There are trolls that will immediately proclaim that if you aren’t for zero then you must be for infinite. In other words, you are either for the complete extinguishment of AI hallucinations or you are relishing AI hallucinations and want them to permeate every inch and quarter of generative AI.
I trust that you can readily discern this all-or-nothing logic is bogus. The sensible realization is that we should indeed strive as mightily as we can to push toward zero instances of AI hallucinations. Period, end of story. At the same time, we should acknowledge that actually attaining zero is probably not in the cards. Accept that we will inevitably be at non-zero, though the desire is to minimize the number and nature of AI hallucinations as best we reasonably can.
Should we toss in the towel if, in fact, we cannot reach an absolute zero count? No, that would be absurd. I say keep up the good work on pursuing AI hallucination reductionism. It still makes abundant sense to find ways to reduce the chances of AI hallucinations arising. Continue to adamantly explore viable mathematical and computational means of either preventing AI hallucinations or at least improving the odds of detecting them in some automatic or axiomatic ways.
There’s more grist for the mill on this thorny matter.
If we cannot reach zero, another hurried exhortation that follows from that gloomy pronouncement is that perhaps we should give up on using generative AI. The seemingly most guaranteed way to avoid AI hallucinations would be to not use generative AI in the first place. Put generative AI up on the shelf of discarded high-tech and let it sit there. It will collect dust until someday we find a kind of computational cure, though that seems unlikely if the notion that AI hallucinations are inevitable holds true.
Well, I have one tried and true catchphrase to say in reply to that way of thinking. You are essentially touting the classic proverb of wanting to toss out the baby with the bathwater. Just because there is a bit of a stink, you want to let everything else be set aside. Once again, flawed logic.
We can live with and prosper in using generative AI that nonetheless clings to the possibilities of emitting AI hallucinations. It will require a willingness on our part to accept the notion that AI hallucinations might occur. One aim will be to minimize the chances of them occurring. Another is to minimize the impacts of them occurring, thus, even if they occur, they will tend toward being trivial or inconsequential. The next aim then becomes how to best detect them at the get-go. Via having reliable and worthy means of detection, we demonstrably aid in refraining from falling into the trap of blindly getting blindsided by AI hallucinations.
Our guard will be up.
Furthermore, the other consideration is to find suitable means to correct AI hallucinations once they have been detected. Detection is the first step. You are alerted that an AI hallucination is in your midst. The second step entails doing something astute about them, either by your hand or by having the generative AI (or other means) do so.
Consider these to be two colossal punches, using all our might to know when they arise and astoundingly knocking them squarely out. Figure out their existence and then mitigate them. Divide and conquer.
The gist is that those waiting on the fence for the day that generative AI will have zero instances of AI hallucinations are waiting for Godot. Turn your attention toward finding the best possible systematic ways to reduce their odds of occurring, reduce their magnitude or impact, and upsize our ability to catch them when they do occur, along with if feasible establishing approaches to overcome or correct them.
I know it hurts to hear this, but I am asking you to accept the nonzero proposition. Ouch. Many are crestfallen. I get that. Sorry to ruin your day. Stew about it for a brief moment. Okay, that’s long enough. Pick yourself up, shake the fog out of your mind, and get to erstwhile work on reduction, detection, and correction.
You can do it.
You have to do it since we must deal with the downsides of generative AI in order to garner the upside benefits that are sorely needed and greatly sought. The world is filled with tradeoffs. When we have limitations or weaknesses, they need to be weighed against the pluses or upsides. I assure you that the opportunities that generative AI provides are not somehow sunk by the dastardliness of AI hallucinations. The prudent ROI (return on investment) calculates that we can live with AI hallucinations, though don’t put our heads in the sand and try to pretend they don’t exist or will magically go away. Have our heads up high and make whatever reasoned efforts we can about them.
Humankind can rise to the challenge.
Now that I’ve laid out the high-level remarks, let’s get into the details.
Digging Into AI Hallucinations
First, I disfavor that the media and even the AI field have adopted the seemingly catchy phrase “AI hallucinations” since the immediate implication is that AI is sentient and hallucinates as humans do, this is an abysmal anthropomorphizing of AI. Sadly, the phrase has become popular, and we are stuck with it for now.
Please know that I hold my nose as I repeat the unfortunate phrase. Others have made earnest attempts at using wording such as AI confabulations, AI errors, AI fiction, and so on. None of those alternatives have the same allure and stickiness. Only a magic wand could overcome the AI hallucination moniker's enormous gravitational pull.
All in all, the crucial takeaway is to not associate today’s generative AI with sentience.
Despite those blaring headlines that seem to claim that we are either at AI sentience or on the verge of it, we aren’t. What fuels the assumption is when we use phrases such as AI hallucinations, which suggests that AI is on par with humans in the hallucinations category. Discard that comparison. Resist the urge to equate the AI of today and human cognition.
Second, the matter is relatively straightforward to describe in that at times generative AI will generate text that we would likely agree is not factual and appears to be made up. There are various reasons that this mathematically and computationally can occur. Efforts are underway to prevent or at least detect made-up or fictitious responses and already progress suggests that the frequency and magnitude of such incidents can be reduced to a significant extent (I’m not saying this is solved, and only emphasizing that it is a known issue, it is being actively worked on, and that incremental progress is being made).
Third, there are a slew of additional issues about generative AI that we should also be concerned about, not just AI hallucinations. Again, for any trolls out there, I am not suggesting we should ignore or downplay the dangers of AI hallucinations. I am merely indicating that we ought to not let AI hallucinations take all the air out of the room. We need to solve or avidly and intelligently pursue a multitude of concerns all at once.
What are some of the mainstay concerns about generative AI overall, you might be wondering?
Today’s generative AI has these selected tendencies that are especially troublesome and deceptive:
- (1) Emits AI hallucinations.
- (2) Conveys a false aura of confidence.
- (3) Lack of explicitly stating uncertainties.
- (4) Lulls you into believing responses are true.
- (5) Uses anthropomorphic wording to mislead you.
- (6) Sneakily portrays humility.
I’ll briefly explore those qualms. Of course, I’ve already touched upon AI hallucinations, item #1 listed, so let’s examine the second bulleted item and then the rest of the points.
Generative AI is purposely devised by AI makers to generate responses that seem confident and have a misleading appearance of an aura of greatness. An essay or response by generative AI convinces the user that the answer is on the up and up. It is all too easy for users to assume that they are getting responses of an assured quality. Now, to clarify, there are indeed times when generative AI will indicate that an answer or response is unsure, but that is a rarity (typically, only occurring when your prompt asks for clarity, see my discussion at the link here). The bulk of the time a response has a semblance of perfection.
Many of the responses by generative AI are really guesses in a mathematical and statistical sense, but seldom does the AI indicate either an uncertainty level or a certainty level associated with an emitted response or dialogue. I’ve noted that via your prompting, you can explicitly request to see a certainty or uncertainty, see my coverage at the link here, but that’s on the shoulders of the user to ask. If you don’t ask, the prevailing default is don’t tell.
Overall, a user is gradually and silently lulled into believing that the generative AI is flawless. This is an easy mental trap to fall into. You ask a question and get a solid answer, and this happens repeatedly. After a while, you assume that all answers will be good. Your guard drops. I’d dare say this happens even to the most skeptical and hardened of users (for a prime example of two lawyers getting snagged by AI hallucinations, see the link here).
Another qualm is how the responses of generative AI are worded. The AI makers have promulgated misleading wording that makes generative AI seem to be sentient. Most answers by the AI will typically contain the word “I” (e.g., “I have your answer for you”, “I was able to complete your request”, or “I am unsure of what you want me to do”). The implication to the user is that the AI is speaking from the heart. We normally reserve the word “I” for humans to use. It is a word bandied around by most generative AI and the AI makers could easily curtail this if they wanted to do so.
It is what I refer to as anthropomorphizing by design (a shameful practice).
Not good.
Yet another concern is that generative AI can produce errors, yet there is often no warning or indication when this occurs. The user must ferret out these mistakes. If it occurs in a lengthy or highly dense response, the chance of discovering the malady is low or at least requires extraordinary double-checking to discover. In a sense, you would be hard-pressed to distinguish between errors and AI hallucinations. They are of a similar caliber in that they are falsehoods, and often are weaved into the responses without any alert or warning they are there.
My other point above is that most generative AI has been specially data-trained to express a sense of humility. See my in-depth analysis at the link here. Users tend to let down their guard because of this artificially crafted humility. Again, this is a trickery undertaken by the AI makers.
Allow me to elaborate on the trickery. In a process such as RLHF (reinforcement learning with human feedback), the initial data-trained generative AI is given added tuning. Personnel are hired to ask questions and then rate the answers of the AI. The ratings are used by the computational pattern matching to fine-tune how later answers should be worded. If you are curious about what generative AI might be like without this fine-tuning, see my discussion at the link here. Included in this process is a ratcheting of the responses from being neutral to instead having an appearance of humbleness.
Some generative AIs such as Grok tend to lean in a different direction, such as being cynical and snarky. One question that as a society we need to consider is whether we want generative AI to be leaned in any particular direction at all. Would we be okay with a neutral variation? Or do we need our generative AI to be humble or perhaps sarcastic? Right now, the marketplace presumably determines this. If users prefer humility, generative AI tuned in that direction will garner usage. If users want cynicism, the generative AI aimed that way will be adopted. And so on.
The overarching takeaway here is that there is a lot of tomfoolery already when it comes to generative AI. You are primed to be taken in by the tricks and techniques being employed. Some of them arise by in a sense happenstance, while others are baked into the pudding.
Let’s get back to our dive into AI hallucinations.
Proposition That AI Hallucinations Are Inevitable
I’d like to first make sure we are on the same page about some basics underlying generative AI, along with establishing allied terminology consisting of making reference to large language models (LLMs).
The way that generative AI customarily works is that a great deal of data is initially fed into a pattern-matching algorithm that tries to identify patterns in the words that humans use. Most of the modern-day generative AI apps were data trained by scanning data such as text essays and narratives that were found on the Internet. Doing this was a means of getting the pattern-matching to statistically figure out which words we use and when we tend to use those words.
Generative AI is built upon the use of a large language model (LLM), which entails a large-scale data structure to hold the pattern-matching facets and the use of a vast amount of data to undertake the setup data training. Note that there are two avenues of largeness involved, namely that the volume of data is large, and the data structure is relatively large too (as an aside, you could also say that the amount of computer processing required is also large, requiring immense computing resources to crunch through everything).
The AI techniques and technology that typically serve at the core of generative AI and LLMs consist of artificial neural networks (ANNs). These are simplistic in comparison to the biological neural networks composing our brains. Do not conflate the two. In the case of artificial neural networks, they are devised in a mathematical way to be a series of computational layers. Various crucial methods have been developed that include transformations of data, attention to certain parts of data, and the like (see my overview of these AI facets at the link here). When you enter prompts into generative AI, the words you enter are converted into numbers (considered to be “tokens), processing occurs on those tokens, and then freshly generated tokens are decoded back into words, for a helpful example of how this works see my discussion at the link here.
There are numerous generative AI apps available nowadays, including GPT-4, Bard, Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, etc. The one that is seemingly the most popular would be ChatGPT by AI maker OpenAI. In November 2022, OpenAI’s ChatGPT was made available to the public at large and the response was astounding in terms of how people rushed to make use of the newly released AI app. There are currently an estimated one hundred million active weekly users of ChatGPT.
I believe that this quick background will sufficiently prepare you for a high-level look at the recent study that analyzed LLMs and generative AI concerning the advent of AI hallucinations. I will be citing excerpts from the study. The paper is available online and is entitled “Hallucination is Inevitable: An Innate Limitation of Large Language Models” by Ziwei Xu, Sanjay Jain, Mohan Kankanhalli, arXiv, January 22, 2024.
Here are some key opener excerpts (don’t worry if these excerpts seem arcane, I’ll explain them):
- “State-of-the-art LLMs are generally implemented using the Transformer architecture, which is a multi-layer feedforward network equipped with attention mechanism. The ‘large’ in LLM describes both the scale of the models, which is usually billions of parameters, and the size of training corpora, which is usually trillions of tokens.” (ibid).
- “However, one of the critical challenges they face is the problem of ‘hallucination,’ where the models generate plausible but factually incorrect or nonsensical information. This issue has brought increasing concerns about safety and ethics as LLMs are being applied widely, resulting in a growing body of literature trying to classify, understand, and mitigate it.” (ibid).
I trust that you readily were able to digest those two opening selected points. The paper notes that generative AI and LLMs are large in data and large in their data structures. In addition, AI hallucinations are a serious problem since they involve the generating of plausible-looking results that are lamentably incorrect or nonsensical. This raises demonstrative safety and ethics concerns. It might be one thing to get AI hallucinations in your generated results if you are just playing around for fun, but if generative AI is used for life-or-death settings such as by medical doctors or in other arenas (see my examples at the link here and the link here), the consequences can be perilously severe.
The next step in the paper consists of defining a formalized mathematical framework for doing a kind of mathematical proof of the type you might have done while taking a math class in college. Sometimes a mathematical framework is so abstract that you would have a difficult time asserting that it applies to the everyday real world. In this instance, the paper states an important premise that if AI hallucinations are found to be inevitable in their simplified mathematical framework, the same can be said that AI hallucinations are also inevitable for real-world LLMs.
Here's what they indicate (excerpts):
- “Hallucination is in essence an erroneous output produced by an LLM. Without getting tangled in the difficult problem of formalizing ‘correctness’ in our real world, we define hallucination in a formal world where all we care about is a computable ground truth function f on S. In other words, in our formal world, f is the ideal function that produces correct completion f(s) for any input string (or prompt, question, query, etc.) s ∈ S.” (ibid).
- “Therefore, if hallucination is inevitable for our LLMs in the relatively simple formal world, then hallucination is inevitable for LLMs in the more complicated real world.” (ibid).
They point out that there are three characteristics of keen interest:
- (a) Total hallucination
- (b) Some hallucination
- (c) Hallucination-free
The first circumstance involves generative AI and LLMs that totally hallucinate nonstop and to the nth degree all the time. That would be extremely disturbing since everything generated would be a so-called hallucination or made-up contrivance. Think of that situation as a never-ending babbling brook.
The second circumstance is what we have today, consisting of hallucinations for some of the time. As I mentioned earlier, we want to minimize that condition.
The third circumstance is our ideal aspiration, the zero condition or being utterly and ironclad hallucination-free. This is a desirable goal. It is a lofty goal. Depending upon what you think of this particular study, it turns out that the zero condition is an unattainable goal in the broad.
Here’s what the paper asserts (excerpts):
- “In this section, we show that hallucination is inevitable in the formal world by suitably applying results in learning theory literature. Specifically, we will use the diagonalization argument in our proof.” (ibid)
- “The high-level idea is to show that any enumeration of an uncountable set is not exhaustive by constructing a counter-example that is in the set but not in the enumeration. The argument gets its name because such a counter-example is constructed by flipping the diagonal elements, i.e., the ith component of the ith element, in the table showing the enumeration.” (ibid).
For those of you deeply into mathematics, you might enjoy their use of a well-known technique known as the diagonalization argument. I am not going to cover the details here. You are encouraged to take a read of the paper if you want to see how they proceed with their mathematical proof.
Based on three theorems that they present; these are the overall conclusions (excerpts):
- “Hallucination is inevitable for P-proved total computable LLMs (Theorem 1). Furthermore, polynomial-time LLMs will hallucinate when solving many real-world problems, including arithmetic’s (Corollary 1).” (ibid).
- “Hallucination is inevitable for LLMs in any computably enumerable set (including the set of P-proved total computable LLMs). All these LLMs could hallucinate on infinitely many inputs (Theorem 2).” (ibid).
- “Hallucination is inevitable for any total computable LLMs (Theorem 3).” (ibid).
- “Since our formal world is a part of the real world, and total computable LLMs are at least as powerful as real-world LLMs, we now conclude with a negative answer to the fundamental question: hallucination of LLMs cannot be eliminated in either our formal world, or in the real world. This answer is independent of (1) LLMs’ architecture and complexity, (2) procedure used to train the LLM, (3) the prompts and questions, (4) the number of training samples, and (5) inference hyperparameters.” (ibid).
The last point above is the proverbial knock-your-socks-off pronouncement. They contend that based on their approach, AI hallucination as a phenomenon cannot be eliminated. They even emphasize that despite any variations in the form or flavor of the generative AI and LLM, the same harsh conclusion is reached.
Drop the mic.
You might remember that at the beginning of this discussion, I said that this is not something we need to become overly despondent about. The real world involves tradeoffs. How many times in your lives have you heard the refrain that sometimes the world takes and sometimes it gives? A lot, I would presume.
The paper also expresses a similar sentiment that we need to consider the intrinsic tradeoffs (excerpt):
- “Although we have shown that LLMs will inevitably hallucinate, this does not undermine their tremendous value in enhancing productivity. Moreover, hallucination itself should not be viewed entirely negatively. In this section, we would like to defend the usage of LLMs and their hallucinatory inclinations.” (ibid).
- “While it is impossible to completely eliminate hallucination, we are optimistic that its severity may be controlled and reduced for many applications.” (ibid).
Turn that sad face you are expressing into a happy face.
We at least know that we have a problem, and we know that we need to do something about it. I’d rather be in that posture than the classic out-of-touch condition of not knowing at all that you have a problem (i.e., it is better to know about what you don’t know, than to not know what you don’t know).
One curious aspect that might get your mind racing along is that they note there could be benefits to having AI hallucinations (excerpt):
- “Finally, hallucination is not completely detrimental. In art, literature, and design, the unintentional and unpredictable outputs from LLMs could inspire human creators. Such deviation from facts can lead to unique perspectives that a strictly factual and precise system might never generate. In this sense, the hallucinatory aspect of LLMs should be regarded positively as a source of inspiration, innovation, and creativity.” (ibid).
I have made a similar insight in a prior column posting that argued perhaps we should consider keeping around some generative AI and LLMs in their rawest of states, see the link here. I ardently indicated that we might find useful the untuned versions, possibly discovering secrets or unbeknownst patterns of human thought as expressed in the vast writings that were pattern-matched on.
These would be completely unfiltered generative AI and LLMs. I went so far as to suggest we might also encompass the said-to-be dark side of the Internet, which is a portion of the Internet that most people do not see since the traditional browsers won’t go there. I do realize that such a devised generative AI and LLM would undoubtedly display the worst of the worst. Somehow, we would need to prevent this from being unduly released such that people might be overcome with shock and dismay.
Regarding the advantages of AI hallucinations, one vexing question is whether those advantages would be leveraged only if we knew when we had one on our hands. In other words, if AI hallucinations occur and we don’t know that it has happened, perhaps we would be unable to recognize the added value it provides.
This brings up the issue of happenstance AI hallucinations versus mandated or hand-spurred AI hallucinations. Here’s what I mean. If you were aiming to have generative AI be inspirational and go outside the box, you might tell the AI to overtly perform an AI hallucination. You were instructing that act to occur.
Some would retort that this is no longer an AI hallucination. They would contend that an AI hallucination is an unforced act. By asking for an AI hallucination, you aren’t really going to get a bona fide AI hallucination. You are getting a contrived result that just so happens to be labeled falsely by you as an AI hallucination.
A bit of a rabbit hole, which I won’t further entertain here.
Conclusion
What are we to do if indeed AI hallucinations are unavoidably inevitable?
I will summarize my suggested path of coping with AI hallucinations that occur in generative AI and LLMs:
- (1) Seek to minimize the frequency of AI hallucinations.
- (2) Aim to minimize the magnitude of AI hallucinations.
- (3) Detect when AI hallucinations have occurred.
- (4) Warn users based on the detection.
- (5) Try to correct a detected AI hallucination.
- (6) Make sure to not overcorrect and make things worse.
If you’d like to see examples of how we might daisy-chain multiple generative AIs together so that the generated results of a primary choice generative AI app are passed through other ones to have them try to ascertain whether an AI hallucination exists, see the link here. This won’t guarantee that you’ll catch all AI hallucinations, but the chances are usually improved by snaring some or many.
For those of you who are smarmy, yes, for such a setup, it is possible that a non-hallucination could be rated as a hallucination by one of the daisy-chain generative AI, and an actual hallucination might not be rated as a hallucination when it really is. Those are the various false positives and false negatives that would be part of the risk model. Thanks for playing.
Another emerging approach consists of the deployment of trust layers, see my discussion at the link here. The idea is that we do a kind of surround sound by enclosing generative AI and LLMs into a layer of added components that do lots of double-checking. The prompts you enter would first be processed by an initial external layer before being passed into the generative AI. Likewise, when the generative AI produces a generated result, it would be passed through the screening layer before being displayed to you.
A plethora of fascinating and promising approaches are being actively pursued.
Time to finish today’s discussion. I’d like to do so with a famous quote from Abraham Lincoln: “You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time.”
We must ensure that AI hallucinations don’t fool anyone for any of the time. If we can’t stop AI hallucinations from ever arising, we should do whatever we can to reduce, detect, and correct. That is a notion that I believe we can all assuredly rally around.

title: Council Post: Three Ways AI Is Changing The Face Of Cybersecurity
text:
Melissa Russell is the executive director of the IEEE Computer Society.
When ranking the technologies most drastically impacting today’s business environment, it comes as no surprise that artificial intelligence (AI) tops the list. In fact, according to a Forbes Advisor survey, 64% of business owners believe that AI will help increase their overall productivity. In addition, PwC reports that 70% of business leaders expect that generative AI will transform how their company creates, delivers and captures value over the next three years.
Even those advancing the technology—the computer science and engineering community—flag growth in generative AI applications and next-generation AI as their top predictions for the year, according to my organization's survey.
All of that rings true, and these statistics lead to a critical application that may just make up AI’s biggest near-term impact: cybersecurity. Not new to the cyber game, fraud-mitigating AI has now matured to a level that is being integrated into standard fraud-prevention systems. And business leaders realize its potential, ranking real-time cybersecurity vulnerability identification and attack prevention as their number one use for AI in 2024 in another survey we conducted.
1. Overall Defense
That’s because AI supports overall digital defense, with nearly seven in 10 businesses indicating their organization plans to leverage it that way. But, at the same time, more than 30% of companies confess that they do not follow standard practices of cyber defense. These developments mean that while businesses now have the power of AI in their employ, success in leveraging it remains dependent on executing good business practices and obtaining the necessary knowledge to harness its potential.
While a robust tool, AI-based cyber solutions are designed to flag anomalies, shore up entry points and screen for targeted attacks. On the other end of that data, there must be a person who can act upon findings to tighten up security protocols. In short, the first line of defense requires the technology to identify and the human to act.
2. Predictive Analytics
But as the adage goes, the best defense is a good offense. That’s where the role of AI in predictive analytics comes into play.
As technology advances, solutions like digital twins—which function as virtual replicas of a physical object, person or process for the purpose of simulation and performance optimization—provide new avenues for AI to prepare for and safeguard more accurately against cyber-attacks.
Digital twin technology can integrate AI tools, bringing together disparate sources of data into a unified model to assess the development, delivery and operation of an asset or an environment. Leveraging this technology will enable systems to advance state-of-the-art predictions, what-if analysis and oversight, supporting businesses in screening proactively against attacks.
3. Managing Misinformation
But just as generative AI offers much potential, so, too, does it provide pitfalls: "Approximately half of executives say that advances in adversarial capabilities (phishing, malware, deepfakes) present the most concerning impact of generative AI on cyber." The spreading of much more realistic misinformation means that companies will need to intensify source checking and critical thinking as they manage activities.
AI-based solutions can help with this identification. As they increase in sophistication, screening technologies can identify nuanced elements that serve as chief indicators of deepfake content.
In addition, many computer science and engineering leaders are focusing on strengthening AI frameworks to protect against this kind of use. With this focus, the goal remains for AI research and development to outpace the potential negative cyber impacts, helping businesses to head off attacks before they are felt.
Where To Start
While AI in cybersecurity has become more widespread and many businesses have already interacted with AI-assisted cyber tools, only half report that they are "very satisfied" with their own cybersecurity capabilities. That means it's time to shore up internal knowledge to better understand the landscape, the threats and the potential solutions.
With that in mind, businesses need to make sure their IT and cyber experts have a handle on how AI is influencing the space and consider hiring additional support if needed. They also can and should lean on their cybersecurity partners to help ensure the latest protections and AI advancements are being integrated and deployed. Finally, they also can look to the computer science and engineering community for solutions and keep abreast of developments in the field.
What Lies Ahead
Continued advances will empower AI technology to evolve to better screen for and prevent cyberattacks, and its accessibility will continue to climb. The industry has but scratched the surface of AI’s potential in cybersecurity. As the computer scientists and engineers at the forefront of its advancements introduce additional solutions, they will fuel the next round of AI-infused innovations to protect the digital environment.

title: Council Post: AI Is Here: Prioritizing Cyber Resilience In 2024 And Beyond
text:
Brian Spanswick is Chief Information Security Officer and Chief Information Officer at Cohesity.
The world of cybersecurity is rapidly evolving. Digital transformation, multi-cloud models and hybrid working are expanding threat surfaces past the perimeter to distributed endpoints, cloud applications and third-party software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms.
The emergence and rapid growth of artificial intelligence, machine learning and large language models (AI/ML/LLM) are making data the most critical asset in an organization as a driver of innovation and productivity. All of this is happening while threat actors use generative AI (GenAI) tools to improve the sophistication of their attacks and lower entry barriers for actors with little or no coding experience. AI/ML/LLMs are strategic imperatives and heightened threats.
These complexities are making it harder than ever for cybersecurity teams to stop every attack at the point of initial access. Threat actors use evasive and adaptive techniques to breach vulnerable threat surfaces and spread, virtually unfettered, across the network in search of targets before delivering their payload.
Unfortunately, existing security approaches that focus solely on prevention are failing to stop this spread or are poorly mitigating the impact of these attacks, causing major disruptions to business operations. Our global cyber resilience survey found that nine in 10 organizations that were victims of ransomware attacks in the past two years had paid a ransom, and two-thirds were willing to pay more than $3 million to recover data and restore business processes.
Organizations can no longer afford to focus solely on prevention. Enterprise security teams must also prioritize minimizing business impact to counter today's highly sophisticated cyber threats. As a result, information security is moving from mainly a compliance and audit responsibility to a core business function—prioritizing cyber resilience as the key to safeguarding organizations from an evolving threat landscape.
A successful cyber resilience strategy will restore an organization's core operations to normal function in a time frame that is consistent with business needs.
Implementing A Robust Cyber Resilience Strategy
Cyber resilience allows organizations to achieve the highest level of operational and business continuity in the face of today's increasingly sophisticated threats and expanding threat surfaces.
Consistent patching, identifying threats and finding vulnerabilities have become table stakes. Cyber resilience requires organizations to predict, withstand and recover from disruptions quickly. An integrated, technical cyber defense that combines exceptional data security and data management helps ensure organizations run optimally in line with business goals and protects their most valuable assets from malicious actors and misuse.
While GenAI tools are making it easier for malicious actors to launch more sophisticated attacks at scale, security teams are also using AI/ML/LLMs to build cyber resilience and counter these adaptive threats. Specifically, they help organizations detect and analyze anomalous behavior to determine the next best steps for remediation. This speeds up the time to detection and time to resolution, allowing security teams to mitigate the impact of breaches.
However, despite the power of AI/ML/LLMs, good, robust cyber resilience can't just be conjured out of thin air. You need a well-thought-out, defined strategy that is closely aligned with your organization's business goals.
Here are three ways you can prioritize cyber resilience in 2024 and beyond.
Align Cyber Resilience To Business Objectives
Cyber resilience isn't about checking boxes on a compliance checklist anymore. It's more nuanced and needs to be tailored for every organization. A software developer doesn't have the same business model as a lumber supplier, so their cyber resilience strategies should focus on mitigating impact on the business according to their organizational goals, market landscape and day-to-day operations.
Formulating and executing the right cyber resilience strategy requires close alignment and collaboration with the full business. Your security team should survey different stakeholders to understand what they need to execute their mission and mitigate potential risks. Which business systems are critical to meeting KPIs? What data is important to them? How will losing that data disrupt their responsibilities or impact customer experience?
Understanding the risk involved in your organization's day-to-day operations helps you train AI/ML/LLMs and make the right cybersecurity decisions for the business.
Collaborate Closely With CIO
Cyber resilience is a boardroom issue, and C-suite involvement and buy-in are critical—starting with the CIO. Data is the lifeblood of business today, and the CIO owns the organization's data strategy, ensuring users have access to the tools and information needed to execute their responsibilities. Work with them to understand data's importance to the organization, the infrastructure and assets that make up the modern data stack, and how to collaborate on safeguarding these critical assets.
It's important to manage the expectations of the C-suite and board on AI/ML/LLM initiatives. Implementing AI/ML/LLMs shouldn't be a mandate itself. These are just tools. They need to be assessed along with other potential solutions to ensure they align with business objectives.
Focus On Minimizing The Impact Of A Breach
Prevention is important, but it shouldn't be the sole strategy for cyber resilience in organizations. Breaches are inevitable; you must be able to detect and stop malicious actors in your environments and then quickly restore and recover impacted operations.
This requires a cybersecurity strategy that is closely aligned with data loss prevention (DLP), backup and recovery and other business continuity capabilities. Getting users and critical business systems back up and running quickly (and securely) after a breach mitigates the impact on the business—allowing you to move forward, deliver products and services and interact with customers.
Strong, Reliable Cyber Resilience To Mitigate The Impact Of Today's Attacks
The evolving cybersecurity landscape requires a rethink of how organizations protect their most critical assets from malicious threats. Mitigating breach impact requires a focus on cyber resilience, switching from a compliance undertaking to more of a critical business function that is closely aligned with the board, the C-suite and other stakeholders across the organization.
While AI/ML/LLMs are enabling more sophisticated attacks at scale, security teams can arm themselves with the same technology to help quickly adapt to these threats. However, organizations must maintain good, reliable cyber resilience to better mitigate the impact these attacks will have on the business.

title: Council Post: GenAI Infrastructure Spend Is Justified By Future Productivity Gains
text:
Rodrigo Madanes is Global Innovation AI Officer at EY.
Generative AI (GenAI) is poised to revolutionize the world in 2024, and it continues to dominate the public conversation. It’s a discussion that is often wide-ranging, covering the innovative promise as well as the potential pitfalls of AI technology. What’s sometimes lost in the churn, though, is an exploration of the economics that currently underpin the development of GenAI infrastructure, in particular, the supply and demand imbalance of these investments.
Consider the significant costs associated with building the necessary supply of GenAI infrastructure, including costly GPU manufacturing and the high energy usage associated with running GenAI tools. However, the demand for this technology—as well as how that demand is likely to materialize—has the potential to far exceed those investments. A number that’s been touted in the media recently (through “back of the napkin” calculations) about the potential level of GenAI investments could be upwards of $200 billion globally by 2025.
How are those levels of investments on the supply side going to be recouped? We expect that demand for GenAI will deliver overall growth and productivity across many industries that will more than justify that investment. We’ve seen in the past how paradigm-shifting technology can have a profound catalytic effect—sometimes in ways that were hard to anticipate initially.
Think of the introduction of electricity; the infrastructure was built for lightbulb usage, but a sizable amount of demand came from newly invented, modern appliances, according to an analysis by Vivek Ramaswami and Sabrina Wu of Madrona Investor Group. Although so much of the current focus on GenAI’s demand looks at content or code generation, who knows what paradigm-shifting use case we are overlooking now?
Quantifying the demand side of the equation is difficult but not impossible. As Guido Appenzeller, former CTO of Intel's Data Center, identified, AI demand won’t simply materialize as AI consumption but instead as general growth—things like marketing, sales and general productivity. With that in mind, the overall impact for a business as large as a Fortune 500 company would be immense. The annual collective revenues for the overall Fortune 500 are about $41 trillion; assuming $200 billion of AI demand (as noted above), this reveals a cost of 0.5%. Given that some GenAI studies have revealed productivity gains of 20-50%, the potential benefits far outweigh the costs for companies looking to embrace AI tools.
But despite the sound economics, companies still have important work to do to take advantage of this moment in AI technology. It’s a race against others, and playing catchup is a difficult exercise when a quick start presents a massive competitive advantage. That means it is essential for businesses to intentionally set up strategies and organizational structures now to carry out pilots and address ethics and compliance issues in an appropriate manner.
These fundamentals are key to deploying and scaling technology like GenAI. A couple of years could make all the difference, leading to significant gains in productivity, having products and offerings marketed more effectively and deploying more insightful AI-enabled assistants.
Moreover, as enterprises further embrace AI projects at scale, managing the costs of compute could be crucial. There’s no one magic bullet; instead, there are multiple areas within the stack that can be addressed to meaningfully reduce expenditures.
One key place is providing the option of GenAI at the user experience (UX) and user interface (UI) layer. Instead of a UI where outputs are automatically generated—something that is intensive from a compute requirement perspective—providing the user a choice would be more efficient. Some users won’t want the GenAI experience, so it is better not to exert the effort or incur the associated costs.
There are other important places to maximize efficiency.
• Large language models (LLMs) have a natural appeal to customers, but companies should embrace LLMs with different levels of quality (and thus compute requirements) depending on business and use cases. This is not a one-size-fits-all option.
• Proprietary models aren’t always the better choice. Open-source LLMs are improving at lightning speed, and given the ease of deploying one in a commonly used cloud, this might be the best bang for your buck.
• And don’t overlook more traditional methods such as optimizing cloud resources. Resisting the impulse to increase your cloud capacity too much is a straightforward but impactful course of action.
These are just a few of the discrete ways you can reduce costs. Taken together, these measures will enable companies to scale GenAI projects without breaking the bank. In a way, it’s a success by a thousand cuts.
In the face of what can feel like the daunting or overwhelming pace of GenAI developments, perhaps it’s worth approaching the challenge in the same way—through a series of tactical steps. The only misguided choice is to simply observe from the sidelines, given the profound implications of this technology. And remember, you don’t have to go about this alone. GenAI is a team sport—stay informed, learn from industry colleagues and embrace technological experts who are closely tracking cutting-edge advances.
The economics of AI infrastructure are sound but do not guarantee success. Be intentional, proactive and mindful of costs to unlock GenAI’s transformative potential.

title: Council Post: Why The Explosion Of LLM Usage Will Drive An Increased Need For NLP
text:
Jeff Catlin, EVP of AI Products, InMoment, the leading provider of integrated Experience Improvement (XI)™ solutions.
The explosive adoption of large language models (LLMs) within all types and sizes of businesses is well-documented and is only accelerating as corporations build their own LLMs based on local LLMs like Meta's Llama 2. An October 2023 Gartner, Inc. survey found that 55% of corporations were piloting or releasing LLM projects, and that number is expected to increase rapidly.
One likely, if unexpected, side effect of this increased usage of LLMs to wrangle the ocean of unstructured data (as much as 90% of a company's data is unstructured) is that natural language processing (NLP) engines will become more important than ever.
I hear a collective question coming: "Wait, won't LLMs mean I won't need NLP anymore?" Sadly, that is not the case—in fact, quite the contrary. LLMs are magical at following someone's lead to answer a question or prompt as well as dig up important, hidden facts and opinions. However, businesses run on metrics, numbers and trends, and you need to be able to dig out all of the relevant metadata to drive your business.
NLP is adept at mining a wide variety of content types and tying them together with common metadata elements such as:
• Named entities: People, companies, places, emails, phone numbers, etc.
• Key concepts: Key ideas within the content (two-word and three-word phrases).
• Categories: Bucketing content into your business language/taxonomy.
• Sentiment: Positive, negative, neutral, mixed.
• Intention: Useful in customer interactions to detect churn, propensity to purchase, etc.
• Effort: Useful in customer support to see how easily a client issue is solved.
There are other extractions beyond these, and all of them help a business tie its disparate information sources together through a common lens—the NLP extractions.
As a software and services vendor that has pioneered machine learning and AI in the customer experience space, we have fully embraced the power of LLMs to change the business landscape. However, we see it as something that will have even more impact on a business when combined with NLP technologies.
A system could show you how your call center agents are doing against your standard metrics. You might notice that the average sentiment of callers from the Northeast is down, so you ask the system to tell you what's driving down customer sentiment in the Northeast. The LLM then answers the question with a few possibilities that you can dig into and verify.
An LLM alone wouldn't alert you to the issue, and NLP alone would be challenged to tell you why sentiment is down. However, the combination will allow business discovery opportunities that were never before possible.
I expect that the need for an ever-more powerful NLP isn't something most people riding the LLM wave have realized yet. Within the next 12 months, however, I believe there will be a renaissance in NLP usage as the value of a combined NLP and LLM-based system becomes apparent. This combination will allow corporate data lakes to fully live up to the promise that data lakes have long been pitching.
An NLP engine is ideal for processing all forms of content within an organization—structured, semi-structured and unstructured—and producing a common key for all content along with metadata like categories, sentiment and such to form a unifying set of content for all of the applications within an organization.
There will be bumps along the way as companies struggle with the heavy cost and hardware requirements along with LLM hallucinations, but the power of NLP-tagged content will allow us to go deeper, examine the LLM assertions and request specific examples of these assertions within the corporate data lake so that we can read and verify the content being used to make these statements.
LLMs aren't coming; they are here, and they will change businesses everywhere. Those businesses that see the value of NLP and LLMs together will be the big winners in this changing world. They will be able to maximize the investments being made in LLMs and will be faster to market with interactive LLM applications that let users investigate their information at a deeper level.
